title: Sell Mineral Rights in Upton County, TX/NM
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Upton County, TX | Spraberry Trend
metaDescription: Own minerals in Upton County near Rankin or McCamey? Get a plain-spoken valuation from someone who reads the Spraberry decline curves, not a form-letter offer.
heroLead: Upton County is quieter than its Midland and Ector neighbors, but the Spraberry Trend runs through it just the same, and the ranching families who've held minerals here for generations often have no idea what a fair number looks like today.
intro: Rankin, the county seat, is a small enough town that everybody knows whose cattle are whose, and a lot of the mineral ownership out here traces back the same way — original ranching-family allotments, split among children and grandchildren, some of whom left West Texas decades ago and haven't thought about the mineral deed since. McCamey, over toward the county's western edge, has its own long oilfield history going back to the 1920s boom.

What's changed in the last several years is that horizontal Spraberry and Wolfcamp development, which built out heavily in neighboring Midland and Reagan counties, has continued to push into Upton County acreage. If your family's minerals have sat quiet for a long time, it's worth checking whether that's still true before assuming the interest isn't worth much.

sections.heading: Rankin, McCamey, and a county built on ranching and oil together
paragraphs: Upton County has never had a large population, and that's kept a lot of its mineral ownership concentrated in the same handful of original ranching families rather than scattered through corporate turnover the way some other Permian counties have. That can be an advantage for owners — records tend to be more traceable when the same names have held the ground for generations — but it also means a lot of interests here are small undivided fractions split among a wide circle of heirs.
McCamey's oil history predates most of the current horizontal boom by nearly a century, and some of the older vertical production out that way is still paying modest, steady checks even now.

sections.heading: Riding the edge of the Spraberry core
paragraphs: Upton County sits along the southern and western edge of the dense Spraberry and Wolfcamp development that's concentrated more heavily in Midland and Martin counties to the north. That edge position means activity here can be more selective — good acreage gets drilled aggressively, while other parts of the county see far less attention.

That's exactly why a fair valuation on an Upton County interest has to start with checking current permits and nearby unit activity on your specific section, not a general sense of how busy the Permian is right now. Two tracts a few miles apart can have very different outlooks.

sections.heading: Small fractional interests are the norm here, not the exception
paragraphs: Because so much of the county's minerals trace back to a handful of original ranching allotments now split among generations of heirs, it's common to run into owners with interests measured in tiny decimals — a 1/64th here, a 1/256th there. These are easy to lose track of and easy to undervalue, since the checks, when they come, are small enough that many owners never bother finding out what the underlying interest itself is worth.

I buy interests of any size. A small fractional interest that's been sitting forgotten in a filing cabinet can still add up to a meaningful lump sum, especially if it sits under acreage that's seeing renewed development.

sections.heading: Getting title straight through the Rankin courthouse
paragraphs: The Upton County clerk's office in Rankin holds records that, for the older ranching-family tracts, can run back the better part of a century. Probate gaps are common where an owner passed without a will, or where heirs never formally recorded their inherited share. None of that is unusual for this county and none of it should discourage you from asking what your interest is worth.
Bring whatever you have, even a decades-old lease or a single check stub, and we'll do the courthouse work to confirm the chain of title before closing.

faqs.question: My family's Upton County minerals haven't paid anything in years. Are they worth selling?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, yes, if there's renewed drilling activity nearby, since a currently non-producing interest can still hold significant value based on future potential. We check current permitting near your specific tract before telling you whether it's worth pursuing.

faqs.question: I only own a small fractional interest, like a 64th or smaller. Do you buy those?
faqs.answer: Yes. Small fractional interests are common in Upton County given how many generations some ranching-family tracts have passed through, and we regularly purchase interests of any size.

faqs.question: Is Upton County actively being drilled right now?
faqs.answer: It sits on the edge of the dense Spraberry and Wolfcamp core to the north, so activity varies more by specific tract than in counties like Martin or Midland. We look at permits and unit activity near your acreage specifically rather than the county as a whole.

faqs.question: My paperwork on this interest is old and incomplete. What do I do?
faqs.answer: Bring what you have — an old lease, a check stub, anything with an owner or well name on it. We use that as a starting point and confirm the rest through Upton County clerk records in Rankin before closing.

faqs.question: Can I sell just my Upton County interest and keep minerals I own elsewhere?
faqs.answer: Yes. We price and close on individual tracts or interests, so you can sell one property while holding onto others in different counties or states.
